'''''Crupina vulgaris''''' is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Asteraceae]]. Its common names include '''common crupina''', '''bearded-creeper''', '''false saw-wort''',<ref name=grin>{{GRIN | accessdate = 12 January 2018}}</ref> and '''starry scabious'''.<ref name=cabi>[http://www.cabi.org/isc/?compid=5&dsid=13697&loadmodule=datasheet&page=481&site=144 ''Crupina vulgaris''.] Invasive Species Compendium. Wallingford, UK: CAB International. 2013.</ref> It is native to parts of [[Europe]], [[Asia]], and [[North Africa]], and it is known elsewhere as an [[introduced species]] and often a [[noxious weed]].<ref name=grin/><ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=108471 Flora of China Vol. 20-21 Page 190 <big>半毛菊属</big> ban mao ju shu ''Crupina'' (Persoon) Candolle]</ref><ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=108471 Flora of North America ''Crupina'' (Persoon) de Candolle]</ref><ref>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/floraspecie.php?genere=Crupina Altervista Flora Italiana, genere ''Crupina'']</ref>

This [[winter annual]] herb produces a slender stem reaching about 120 cm (4 feet)<ref name=jeps>[http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_IJM.pl?tid=2430 ''Crupina vulgaris''.] The Jepson eFlora 2013.</ref><ref name=burke>[http://biology.burke.washington.edu/herbarium/imagecollection.php?Genus=Crupina&Species=vulgaris ''Crupina vulgaris''.] Burke Museum. University of Washington.</ref> in height. The ridged stem has many branches, and is leafy below. The basal leaves are entire, toothed, or divided, and have rough-haired surfaces and bristly edges. They generally wither by flowering. Leaves higher on the stem are up to 3.5 centimeters long and are divided into narrow lobes with bristly edges. The slender [[pseudanthium|flower head]] is about 1 or 2 centimeters long. It contains up to 5 florets, usually only one of which is fertile. It has a purple [[Corolla (flower)|corolla]]. It yields one large fruit, a [[Asteraceae#Fruits and seeds|cypsela]] up to 1.6 centimeters long including its barrel-shaped body and its long, spreading [[pappus (flower structure)|pappus]] of brown or black bristles.<ref name=fna>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200023809 ''Crupina vulgaris''.] Flora of North America.</ref> It can weigh up to 36 milligrams.<ref name=cabi/> One average plant produces about 130 fruits.<ref name=cdfa>{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20121213020043/http://www.cdfa.ca.gov/plant/ipc/weedinfo/crupina.htm|title=''Crupina vulgaris''.}} Encycloweedia. California Department of Food and Agriculture.</ref>

The [[flower heads]] often fall off the plant after the seeds ripen, each containing one fruit, or occasionally two in heads that produced two fertile florets. The seeds fall out and are [[seed dispersal|dispersed]] by the wind or on the feet of [[livestock]]; they can be dispersed greater distances when floating on water or when transported by rodents, birds, or humans,<ref name=cdfa/> including on machinery and in contaminated shipments of [[hay]] or grain.<ref name=ca>[http://www.inspection.gc.ca/plants/plant-protection/invasive-plants/fact-sheets/crupina-vulgaris-/eng/1331733358077/1331733427684 ''Crupina vulgaris'' Cass. (common crupina) - Fact Sheet.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029204835/http://www.inspection.gc.ca/plants/plant-protection/invasive-plants/fact-sheets/crupina-vulgaris-/eng/1331733358077/1331733427684 |date=2013-10-29 }} Canadian Food Inspection Agency.</ref> The seeds can pass unscathed through the guts of most animals, except [[sheep]].<ref name=cdfa/> The [[cotyledon]]s of the seedling have a bright purple<ref name=id>[http://www.oneplan.org/crop/noxweeds/nxWeed04.asp ''Crupina vulgaris''.] Idaho's Noxious Weeds. Idaho OnePlan. University of Idaho.</ref> red,<ref name=cabi/> or purplish red midvein and margins.<ref name=cdfa/>

The plant can grow in a range of temperatures, moisture levels, and soil types,<ref name=cdfa/> and in many types of habitat, including [[field (agriculture)|field]]s, [[pasture]]s, [[grassland]]s, roadsides, railroads, and dump sites.<ref name=ca/> It is not [[invasive species|invasive]] in its native range, but in regions where it has [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]], such as the rangelands of the western United States, it can negatively affect native flora through [[Competition (biology)|competition]], reduce the quality of [[forage]], and increase soil [[erosion]].<ref name=cabi/> The plant can form wide stands in fields. It is unpalatable to most grazing animals, which avoid it and selectively consume other grasses and herbs, allowing the weed to survive and spread.<ref name=cdfa/> Sheep and [[goat]]s will consume the plant, but are not effective agents of eradication.<ref name=cabi/>

A number of natural enemies have been recorded, such as the [[mite]] ''[[Aceria balasi]]'', which attacks the [[inflorescence]], the [[moth]]s ''[[Clytie illunaris]]'', ''[[Metzneria aprilella]]'', and ''[[Ornativalva plutelliformis]]'', which feed on the seeds, and the [[weevil]] ''[[Styphlus penicillus]]'', which feeds on the leaves.<ref name=cabi/> ''[[Ramularia crupinae]]'', first described from the plant, is a [[pathogenic fungi|pathogenic sac fungus]] that grows on its leaves.<ref name=cabi/> No agents of [[biological pest control]] have been established.<ref name=cdfa/>
